title.rendered: Travel Marketing in Canada: How Sponsorship, Linear TV and Digital Reach Qualified Travellers

excerpt.rendered: Travel marketing in Canada works best when sponsorship, linear TV and digital channels work together. See how to reach qualified travellers and drive bookings.

content.rendered:
Travel marketing works best when it reaches people the moment they start picturing a trip and stays with them until they book. In Canada, the most effective approach pairs sponsorship and linear television, which build trust and scale, with digital channels, which add precision and measurement. Used together, they put a destination, resort, cruise line or tour operator in front of qualified travellers: people with the means, the interest and the intent to book.

Travel is one of the most considered purchases a household makes. The planning window runs for weeks or months, several people weigh in, and the final choice is as emotional as it is practical. The brands winning share are the ones present across the whole journey, not only at the final click.

Why travel marketing is different from other categories

Most advertising asks for a quick decision. Travel asks for a big one. A couple choosing between a river cruise and a week in Maui will compare options, read reviews, talk to a travel advisor and often change their minds before committing. Along the way they are influenced by what they see on television, in their social feeds, in search results and in their inbox.

This changes how a campaign should be built. A single channel can start the conversation, but it rarely finishes it. Travel marketing needs a plan covering inspiration, consideration and booking, with each channel doing the job it does best.

Start with the qualified traveller, not the mass audience

Reach is only valuable when it reaches the right people. A qualified traveller has the household income to afford the trip, a history of travelling, and a life stage which fits the product. Empty nesters planning a cruise, families looking at a ski week and professionals booking a long weekend escape are three very different buyers.

Origin market matters just as much. A sun destination selling to Canadians will focus on the cities with direct flights, such as Vancouver, Calgary, Edmonton, Toronto and Montreal. Defining these audiences before buying any media is what separates efficient travel advertising from expensive noise. For a broader view of traveller sentiment, Destination Canada publishes research worth reviewing during planning.

Travel sponsorship: borrowing trust from programming Canadians already watch

Sponsorship is one of the most powerful tools in travel marketing because it attaches your brand to content viewers already trust. A weather sponsorship on a local newscast, a branded travel segment on a morning show or a presence inside live sports places your destination alongside programming people choose to watch every day.

The value goes beyond the airtime. Viewers tend to accept sponsored content as part of the program rather than an interruption, so the message lands with more credibility than a standard spot. For travel brands, sponsorship also opens the door to storytelling: a resort walkthrough, an interview with a tour operator or a destination feature can show the experience in a way a 30-second ad rarely can.

Linear television: scale and credibility for travel brands

Linear television remains the fastest way to build broad awareness in a Canadian market. Local news, morning shows, live sports and prime-time programming put your brand in front of an entire city at once, with sight, sound and motion bringing a destination to life. Travel is a visual product, and few screens sell a beach, a mountain or a ship deck better than the biggest one in the house.

Television also carries authority. Travellers spending a significant amount on a trip want reassurance the brand is established, and being seen on a trusted network provides exactly this. We cover the medium in more depth in Is Television Advertising Still Worth It in 2026?

Media Buying

Digital channels: precision through the booking journey

Where linear builds demand, digital channels capture and convert it. Connected TV and streaming reach the growing audience who no longer watch traditional broadcast, with targeting by geography, household and interest. Paid social on Meta and Instagram puts immersive video and photography in front of travellers while they scroll for ideas. Google Search captures intent the moment someone types a phrase like “all-inclusive resorts from Vancouver.”

Retargeting keeps your brand present for travellers who visited your site but did not book, and email nurtures them through a long planning window. Each digital touchpoint can be measured, refined and scaled based on what produces bookings.

Streaming

How linear and digital work together in travel marketing

The strongest travel campaigns treat linear and digital as one plan rather than two budgets. A sponsorship or television flight creates a spike in awareness, which shows up as a lift in branded search and site traffic. Digital campaigns then retarget those visitors, extend reach through streaming to cord-cutters and push qualified prospects towards a booking. Our approach to combining channels is outlined in Media Buying in Canada.

A consistent creative system holds it all together. The same imagery, offer and message should appear on television, in streaming, in social and on the landing page, so every touchpoint reinforces the last. When the pieces connect, each channel makes the others more efficient.

Measuring travel marketing beyond the click

Travel decisions happen over time and across devices, so measurement has to look beyond last-click attribution. Useful signals include lifts in branded search, traffic to a dedicated landing page, booking engine conversions, promo code redemptions, completed view rates on streaming, inquiries to travel advisors and brand lift studies.

Building this measurement into the plan from day one is what turns a travel campaign into a learning system. Our process is outlined in Inside the Media Buying Process: Six Steps From Brief to Optimization.

Common mistakes in travel advertising

The same issues come up again and again. Brands spread a modest investment across too many channels and never reach the frequency needed to be remembered. Campaigns launch too close to departure, after most travellers have already decided. Creative relies on generic stock imagery rather than the real experience. Travel advisors, who still influence a large share of bookings, get left out of the plan. And ads send interested travellers to a homepage rather than a landing page built to convert.

Each of these is easy to fix with planning, and fixing them often improves results more than adding budget.

The bottom line

Effective travel marketing in Canada combines the trust of sponsorship, the scale of linear television and the precision of digital channels into one coordinated plan. Done well, it reaches qualified travellers early, stays with them through a long decision and turns interest into bookings you can measure.
